title: 07 — Design a Unique ID Generator in Distributed Systems
html:
07 — Design a Unique ID Generator in Distributed Systems

The one idea: a single auto-increment column can't keep up across many databases. Twitter's Snowflake packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits: IDs are unique without coordination, roughly time-sortable, and fit in a bigint.

Step 1 — Scope

  • IDs must be unique and numeric, fit in 64 bits.
  • Ordered by date (IDs created later are larger — at least roughly).
  • Generate 10,000+ IDs per second.

Step 2 — Options

Approach How Pros Cons
Multi-master auto-increment k DB servers, each increments by k (server 1: 1, 1+k, 1+2k…) Uses the DB, numeric Hard to scale up/down; not time-ordered across servers
UUID v4 128 random bits generated locally No coordination, trivial 128 bits; not sortable; poor B-tree index locality
Ticket server One DB hands out IDs (Flickr) Numeric, simple SPOF; multiple ticket servers bring back sync issues
Snowflake 64 bits: timestamp + machine + sequence Unique, sortable, 64-bit, no coordination Depends on clock correctness

Choose Snowflake for the requirements given.

Step 3 — Deep dive: the Snowflake layout

| 1 bit | 41 bits              | 5 bits        | 5 bits     | 12 bits  |
| sign  | timestamp (ms)       | datacenter ID | machine ID | sequence |
Field Size Meaning
Sign 1 Always 0 (keeps the ID positive)
Timestamp 41 Milliseconds since a custom epoch (e.g. the system's launch date) — lasts ~69 years
Datacenter ID 5 32 data centres
Machine ID 5 32 machines per DC
Sequence 12 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine; resets every ms

Throughput: 4,096 × 1,000 = ~4M IDs/s per machine.

public sealed class SnowflakeIdGenerator
{
    private static readonly long Epoch = new DateTimeOffset(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero).ToUnixTimeMilliseconds();
    private readonly long _workerId;          // datacenter (5 bits) + machine (5 bits)
    private long _lastTimestamp = -1;
    private long _sequence;
    private readonly object _gate = new();

    public SnowflakeIdGenerator(int datacenterId, int machineId) =>
        _workerId = ((long)datacenterId << 5) | (uint)machineId;

    public long NextId()
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            long now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds();

            if (now < _lastTimestamp)
                throw new InvalidOperationException("Clock moved backwards; refusing to generate IDs.");

            if (now == _lastTimestamp)
            {
                _sequence = (_sequence + 1) & 0xFFF;           // 12 bits
                if (_sequence == 0)                            // exhausted this ms → wait for next
                    while ((now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()) <= _lastTimestamp) { }
            }
            else
            {
                _sequence = 0;
            }

            _lastTimestamp = now;
            return ((now - Epoch) << 22) | (_workerId << 12) | _sequence;
        }
    }
}

Step 4 — Wrap-up: what to discuss

  • Clock synchronisation: machines disagree on time; NTP adjustments can move a clock backwards. Options: refuse and wait, or keep a logical "last timestamp" and continue from it.
  • Assigning machine IDs: static config, or lease them from ZooKeeper/etcd/a DB table at startup — two machines with the same ID generate duplicates.
  • Section tuning: fewer sequence bits + more timestamp bits suits low-concurrency, long-lived systems.
  • High availability: the generator is in-process or a small stateless service — it's as available as its host.
  • Ordering caveat: IDs are sorted by time per machine; across machines they're only roughly ordered (clock skew).

Alternatives worth naming

Format Size Notes
UUID v7 (RFC 9562) 128 bits Timestamp-prefixed, so index-friendly; no worker ID coordination needed
ULID 128 bits Time + randomness, Crockford base32 string, sortable
KSUID 160 bits Seconds timestamp + 128 random bits

If 128 bits is acceptable, UUID v7 removes the machine-ID problem entirely and is the modern default.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • .NET 9+: Guid.CreateVersion7() — sortable, index-friendly GUIDs out of the box.
  • SQL Server: NEWSEQUENTIALID() (sequential per machine, restarts after reboot), SEQUENCE objects with CACHE, or bigint IDENTITY. Random NEWID() as a clustered key causes page splits and fragmentation.
  • EF Core: sequential GUID generation for SQL Server is the default for Guid keys (SequentialGuidValueGenerator).
  • Worker IDs on AKS: derive from the StatefulSet ordinal (pod-0, pod-1…) — stable and unique.
  • Community package: IdGen implements Snowflake-style IDs for .NET.

Review checklist

  • Requirements: unique, 64-bit, time-ordered, throughput.
  • Compare at least three approaches with trade-offs.
  • Bit layout and the math (69 years, 4,096/ms).
  • Clock-backwards handling.
  • How machine IDs are assigned uniquely.
  • Mention UUID v7 if 128 bits is allowed.
